implementation_notes: Preferred modern realization: choose the library's non-throwing overload that reports through a std::error_code& out-parameter and simply do not inspect it (`std::filesystem::remove(p, ec)` is noexcept), so no exception is ever raised and the ignore is an unused output value rather than a swallowed throw. The same shape exists for other standard operations with an ec parameter, and it keeps the mute out of the exception path entirely.
pitfalls: An unused error_code out-parameter is easy to mistake for an unchecked one; name it, comment it, or the next reader turns it back into a throwing call.
Error-code overloads are not uniformly available, so mixing them with throwing calls of the same operation makes the ignore look accidental.
`ec` is assigned on failure only; a stale value from a previous call must not be read as the current outcome - clear it or scope it to the call.

variants.name: Explicit (void) cast of a [[nodiscard]] result
variants.implementation_notes: Where the call returns an error indicator rather than throwing, C++17's [[nodiscard]] turns an accidental discard into a compiler warning, so the deliberate one has to be written as a cast to void - the standard-library convention for 'the result is intentionally unused' - with the reason in a comment. Use it when no error_code overload exists and when a file-wide warning suppression would hide future mistakes.
pitfalls: The cast silences the warning for that expression permanently: if the call later becomes load-bearing, nothing flags it again.
`((void)x)` style macros and pragma-based suppressions hide the intent instead of stating it - keep the discard per call site and visible.
A void cast only silences the warning; it does not defer or handle the failure, so the surrounding function must still be sound if the call did nothing.
